summary: Since the TRILL base protocol was published in 2011, deployment has revealed errata in RFC 6325 and areas needing clarification. This standards-track RFC gathers corrections, clarifications and updates for it. It updates RFC 6325, RFC 7177 and RFC 7179.

eli5.summary: After a big rulebook has been in use for a while, people find mistakes and unclear parts. This is the list of fixes and clearer wording.

subtitle: A bundle of fixes, clarifications and small extensions for the TRILL base protocol, five years after it appeared.

tldr.problem: After the TRILL base protocol (RFC 6325) was published in 2011, deployment and development exposed errors in the text and areas that needed clarification or updating.
tldr.mechanism: This document collects the known corrections, clarifications and updates in one place: overload handling, distribution tree rules, nickname selection, MTU rules, IS-IS flooding support, a larger Hop Count and a few new header bits.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 7180, updates RFC 6325, RFC 7177 and RFC 7179, and in any conflict with those documents it takes precedence. It is itself updated by RFC 8249.

sections.title: Why This Document Exists
sections.content:
TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links) lets RBridges, also called TRILL switches, route traffic across a campus of links. The base protocol is RFC 6325, published in 2011. Active development and deployment then revealed errors in it and several places that needed clarification or updates.

Other documents already cover adjacency (RFC 7177), the ESADI protocol (RFC 7357) and Appointed Forwarders (a replacement for RFC 6439). This document supplies the other known fixes. It obsoletes RFC 7180, the previous collection of this kind, and updates RFC 6325, RFC 7177 and RFC 7179.

If this document conflicts with any of those three, this document takes precedence. It also fixes the precedence order among the sections of RFC 6325 as 4 > 3 > 7 > 5 > 2 > 6 > 1, to be used only as a fallback if a conflict is ever found. Each section is tagged New, Changed or Unchanged so readers can see which technical material is genuinely new. One change, the numbering of distribution trees, is not backward compatible with RFC 6325.
sections.eli5: A rulebook for a big game was printed years ago. Players found typos and fuzzy rules, so this new sheet fixes them, and if the two ever disagree, the new sheet wins.

sections.title: Overloaded and Unreachable RBridges
sections.content:
An RBridge can be in overload, shown by the IS-IS overload flag in its link-state PDUs (LSPs). Either it cannot hold the whole link-state database, or it was configured that way, which is a common practice during maintenance. Packets are not least-cost routed through an overloaded switch, although they may start or end there. Links with cost 2**24 - 1 are likewise avoided and reserved for traffic-engineered packets. An RBridge that can be reached only through such links or switches is called data unreachable.

An overloaded RBridge cannot be trusted to compute distribution trees or the reverse path forwarding check correctly, so it can appear only as a leaf of a multi-destination tree. When a unicast packet for an unknown egress nickname arrives, it MUST NOT discard it for that reason. It MUST try to forward it to a non-overloaded neighbor chosen at random, and discards it only if there is none. For multi-destination packets it MUST NOT apply the reverse path check and MUST NOT forward them, except by egressing native frames where it is Appointed Forwarder.

For frames an overloaded RBridge originates itself, known unicast goes to any neighbor that is not overloaded. Multi-destination frames use the OOMF (Overload Originated Multi-destination Frame) service. A neighbor offers it by setting a bit in its TRILL Hellos for that RBridge. The overloaded switch tunnels the frame to the neighbor, which rewrites the egress nickname to a distribution tree it uses, sets the M bit and forwards it. The overloaded switch MUST NOT also distribute the frame locally in native form, since that would deliver it twice. If no neighbor offers OOMF, it MUST distribute the frame locally where it is Appointed Forwarder.

The provider of OOMF service MAY rate-limit it. The RFC notes that even limited bandwidth can matter for bootstrapping services such as DHCP and ARP/ND at the overloaded switch.
sections.eli5: Imagine a classroom helper who is too swamped to pass notes properly. Instead of dropping the notes, they hand them to a neighbor who is not swamped, and the neighbor passes them on.

sections.title: Distribution Trees and the RPF Check
sections.content:
Several corrections concern the trees used for broadcast, unknown-unicast and multicast traffic. The number of trees an RBridge computes is corrected to up to k if j is zero, or the minimum of j and k if j is non-zero. Tree numbering is changed so the selected parent is (j-1) mod p instead of the old rule, so that with two trees and two possible parents, tree 1 picks parent 0 and tree 2 picks parent 1. This is not backward compatible, and if RBridges disagree the reverse path check will drop many multi-destination packets. Link costs may be asymmetric, but all RBridges must use the cost from the tree root R to the node N, not N to R.

RFC 7780 also allows a stronger RPF check. The RFC 6325 check validates the triplet of ingress nickname, tree and input port. On a multi-access link, a transient topology change can make a node receive duplicates of every multi-destination packet even though both that check and the separate tree adjacency check pass. The stronger check validates the quadruplet of ingress nickname, source SNPA (the Outer.MacSA on Ethernet), tree and input port. It costs more state when a switch has several ports on one link, and can cause more transient packet loss, so it is optional.

TRILL switches MUST implement either the RFC 6325 checks or the stronger check for multi-destination packets. A campus can mix the two.
sections.eli5: A tree is a map of who passes a message to whom, so everyone gets one copy. If helpers use different maps, copies get lost or doubled, so everybody has to count the same way.

sections.title: Nickname Selection
sections.content:
Each RBridge picks a 16-bit nickname. If two RBridges choose the same nickname x, the one with the numerically higher priority keeps it. On a tie, the higher 7-byte IS-IS ID (LAN ID) wins, and the other RBridge MUST select a new one. This corrects an erratum in RFC 6325, which named the wrong fields.

When checking for conflicts, nicknames held by IS-IS unreachable switches MUST be ignored, but those held by IS-IS reachable switches MUST NOT be ignored, even if they are data unreachable. When choosing a new nickname, an RBridge SHOULD prefer one that no switch appears to hold, reachable or not. It MUST keep monitoring for conflicts after it has a nickname, even while in overload.

In the unlikely case that all valid nicknames, 0x0001 through 0xFFBF, are in use with higher priority by reachable switches, an RBridge without a nickname cannot be an ingress, egress or tree root, but it still works as a transit switch.
sections.eli5: Everyone in the room needs a unique name tag. If two kids pick the same one, a simple rule decides who keeps it, and the other picks again.

sections.title: MTU and Port Modes
sections.content:
TRILL derives its size limits from originatingL1LSPBufferSize. The campus-wide value Sz is the minimum across the RBridges, but not less than 1470. In Layer 3 IS-IS the default is 1492 bytes, while in TRILL it defaults to 1470 bytes, leaving 27 bytes of headroom for legacy devices with the classic Ethernet maximum despite headers such as an Outer.VLAN. TRILL Hello PDUs MUST NOT exceed 1470 bytes. Sz does not limit TRILL Data packets, which are limited only by the links they cross.

Three MTU errata in RFC 6325 are corrected. Multi-destination MTU-probe and MTU-ack PDUs MUST go to the All-IS-IS-RBridges multicast address. These PDUs MAY also be unicast, which RFC 6325 had wrongly excluded. The MTU test compares against Sz using greater than or equal, not strictly greater than.

The document also adds a table showing exactly which frame types each combination of the four port mode bits allows, and explains that the CFI bit in the inner VLAN tag became the DEI (Drop Eligibility Indicator) bit in IEEE 802.1Q-2011. TRILL switches with ports following that standard MUST carry the DEI value through ingress, transit and egress.
sections.eli5: Mailboxes only take envelopes up to a certain size. This part says exactly how big the control messages may be and fixes a rule that was off by one.

sections.title: The Updated TRILL Header
sections.content:
The TRILL Header has been changed over time by RFC 6325, RFC 7455 and RFC 7179, and this document updates it again. The first word holds Version (V), Alert (A), Color (C), Multi-destination (M), four reserved bits, the F bit and a 6-bit Hop Count, followed by the Egress and Ingress Nicknames and an optional flags word. The old header-extension length field, Op-Length, is replaced by the reserved bits and the F bit. If F is non-zero, the flags word is present. A switch MUST ignore the A and C bits when hashing for equal-cost multipath.

The Color bit lets an ingress switch mark packets for implementation-specific uses such as traffic studies. Transit switches MUST NOT change it. The reserved bits MUST be sent as zero, and a switch receiving a packet with any of them set MUST discard it unless it understands a future use.

The Extended Hop Count option uses flags word bits 14 through 16 to make the Hop Count 9 bits wide, raising the maximum from 64 to 512. Reliable use above 64 generally needs support at every switch on the path, which switches advertise with bit 14 of the TRILL version sub-TLV capabilities. The high-order 3 bits go in the flags word and the low-order 5 bits stay in the base header. Flags word bits 27 and 28 form a 2-bit Extended Color field, also for implementation-specific marking.
sections.eli5: The header is the label on a parcel. The new rules let the label say that a parcel may hop through many more stops, and add a color sticker for the post office's own use.

sections.title: IS-IS Flooding and Other Control Changes
sections.content:
TRILL switches MUST support Extended Level 1 Flooding Scope (E-L1FS) PDUs from RFC 7356. They MUST also include a Scope Flooding Support TLV in every TRILL Hello and advertise an E-L1FS capability bit, called the E bit, in the TRILL version sub-TLV. E-L1FS increases the number of fragments available for link-state information by over two orders of magnitude. Because of this, RFC 7177 is updated so that the Scope Flooding Support TLV is part of the adjacency data and the TRILL Hello contents. In a mixed campus, only four sub-TLVs (Interested VLANs, VLAN Group, Interested Labels and Label Group) may be advertised in E-L1FS, and only if all interested switches support it and are connected through E-L1FS-capable switches.

Other changes in this group:

  • Control packets that establish and maintain adjacency (Hello, MTU-probe, MTU-ack) SHOULD get the highest priority, so a flood of other traffic cannot break adjacency.
  • PDUs with unknown PDU numbers MUST be silently discarded, and a per-number counter is advised.
  • The optional NickFlags APPsub-TLV, type 6, lets a switch say which of its nicknames it may use as an ingress. It is ignored if its length is not a multiple of 4.
  • Switches SHOULD support graceful restart from RFC 5306 and SHOULD include the Purge Originator Identification TLV in purge PDUs.

The Appointed Forwarder Status Lost Counter may be left at zero or aligned with adjacent VLANs in cases where data-plane learning is unused or Appointed Forwarder status is irrelevant, so that VLAN sub-TLVs can be aggregated.
sections.eli5: The switches get a bigger notebook for sharing news, a rule to answer urgent messages first, and a way to say which of their names they use when sending.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says that general TRILL security considerations stay in RFC 6325. This document corrects six errata, improves the documentation and does not change those considerations, with two exceptions.

First, E-L1FS FS-LSPs can be authenticated with IS-IS security (RFC 5310), by including an IS-IS Authentication TLV in E-L1FS PDUs. Second, when the allowed weaker RPF check is used, multi-destination packets can be duplicated under very rare topologies and transient conditions, which could have security consequences for some protocols.
sections.eli5: The old safety rules still apply. The new notebook can be locked with a password, and one old counting shortcut can sometimes hand out a copy twice.
